# Translate a Foreign Menu or Sign Right from Your iPhone Camera

> **In short:** Point your iPhone camera at any foreign text — a menu, a sign, a museum plaque — and watch it turn into English on screen in seconds. With Apple Intelligence on iPhone 15 Pro or newer, the translation can appear automatically before you tap anything.

Standing in a small restaurant in Tokyo, you hold the menu upside down and smile apologetically. Sound familiar? Your iPhone can read it for you, right now, in your pocket — you just need to know which button to press.

## Before you start
- An **iPhone running iOS 16 or newer** for the basic Camera translation (most iPhones from the last few years).
- For the **automatic, hands-free translation** powered by Apple Intelligence (Live Translation), you need an **iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model**, with Apple Intelligence turned on in Settings.
- The **Camera** and **Translate** apps, both already on your iPhone.
- A working **internet connection** the first time you translate a new language — after that, several languages work offline.
- About **30 seconds per translation** once you get the hang of it.

## Step 1 — Open the Camera app

Find the **Camera** app on your Home Screen — the icon looks like a small camera lens. You can also **swipe left on the Lock Screen** to open it instantly without unlocking. Tap once. The viewfinder opens, showing whatever is in front of your rear camera.

If you accidentally open the front (selfie) camera, look for a small **curved arrow icon** 🔄 near the shutter button and tap it to flip back to the rear lens — the rear lens is the one that "reads" text well.

You'll know it worked when the live view fills the screen and you can see the room around you.

## Step 2 — Point your iPhone at the foreign text

Hold the phone steady, about **6–12 inches (15–30 cm)** from the words you want translated. A menu, a street sign, a book page, a museum placard — all of these work. Slowly tilt or move closer until the words look crisp on screen.

If the text is small, on a curve (a coffee cup, a bottle), or behind glass, move a little closer. If the image looks shaky or blurry, **tap once directly on the words** — that forces the camera to focus on them.

You'll know it worked when the text on screen looks sharp and a small icon appears in the bottom-right corner that looks like **three lines of text inside a square**.

💬 Example: aim at a French menu line that reads "Soupe à l'oignon, 8€" — once the camera focuses, the icon pops up.

## Step 3 — Tap the Live Text indicator (or wait for Apple Intelligence)

That little **lines-in-a-square icon** is Apple's way of saying: "I see words here, and I can read them." Tap it once. The text on screen highlights in a soft yellow or blue color, as if someone ran a highlighter across each word.

If you have an iPhone 15 Pro or newer with Apple Intelligence turned on, you may see the translation appear **automatically**, without even tapping — the phone recognizes the language and offers the English version right on top of the original. If that happens, jump ahead to Step 5.

If nothing appears, try moving the camera an inch closer or farther, or tap the words directly to wake up the detection.

You'll know it worked when the words on screen are highlighted in color.

## Step 4 — Choose Translate from the pop-up menu

Once the words are highlighted, a small menu appears near your finger. It usually shows options like **Copy**, **Look Up**, **Share**, and — the one you want — **Translate**. Tap **Translate**.

A translation panel slides up from the bottom of the screen. The original text sits on top; the English version appears just below it.

If your phone's main language is something other than English, the panel might show that language first. Tap the **language name at the top** of the panel to switch the output to English.

You'll know it worked when you see two versions of the same text — the original and the English — stacked together.

💬 Example: pointing at "Soupe à l'oignon, 8€" should give you "Onion soup, 8€" in well under a second.

## Step 5 — Read the translation at your own pace

The English text stays on screen as long as you keep the Camera app open. Read it slowly. Tilt the phone a little to compare the original and the translation side by side. If the camera loses focus, just point back at the text and the translation reappears.

Two honest limits worth knowing: very stylized fonts (the fancy cursive on wedding invitations), handwriting, and faded old signs can confuse the camera. And the translation is excellent for everyday language — restaurant dishes, signs, simple instructions — but it can stumble on poetry, slang, or very technical medical or legal terms.

You'll know it worked when you can read the English meaning clearly without typing a single word.

## Step 6 — Save a photo if you want to keep the translation

If you'd like a permanent copy — for a trip diary, to share with a friend, or to look up later — press the **round white shutter button** at the bottom of the screen. The photo saves to your Photos app.

Later, when you open that photo, you'll see the same Live Text icon in the corner. Tap it, choose **Translate**, and the English version pops up again — even without internet.

If you only needed the translation for right now, just **swipe up from the bottom** to close the Camera app, or press the Home button. Nothing is saved, nothing to delete later.

You'll know it worked when a small thumbnail appears in the bottom-left corner of the Camera screen.

## Common mistakes

- **Holding the phone too far away.** Live Text needs to see the letters clearly. If no icon appears, move closer — about the distance between your hand and a paperback book is usually right.
- **Pointing at glossy or curved surfaces.** Text on a wine bottle, a coffee cup, or behind glass can be hard to read. Try straightening the angle or moving the phone a few inches to one side to kill the glare.
- **Expecting perfect translations of menus.** The camera is great for everyday dishes ("soup," "beef stew"), but poetic restaurant names and ingredient lists sometimes come out funny. When in doubt, point at two or three items and use the context to figure out the rest.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** you can read signs, instructions, and labels on the go — at airports, train stations, pharmacies, and grocery stores — without typing or copy-pasting anything.
- **For your travel or work:** if you travel, host visitors, or work with people who speak another language, this turns your iPhone into a quiet, polite translator. Show the translation on the screen instead of fumbling with phrasebooks.
- **If you're just getting started:** try the easiest thing first — point at one piece of text in a book, magazine, or product label, and watch it turn into English. That's the whole trick.

## Try it now

Grab any book, magazine, or product label with words on it. Open the Camera app, point at the words, and tap the little **lines-in-a-square** icon when it appears in the corner. You'll have a translation in under five seconds.
